text:
I have been waiting almost 3 years to write these words:

NO EVIDENCE OF DISEASE. 🙏❤️

Today we met with Braelyn’s neurosurgeon, Dr. Linda Liau at UCLA (telehealth). 

When our local radiologist read Braelyn’s August 28 MRI as “no evidence of disease recurrence,” we were thrilled—but I was afraid to fully exhale.

I knew Dr. Liau and the UCLA tumor board would scrutinize every millimeter of those images.

What if they saw something the local radiologist missed?

Today, Dr. Liau told us that she and the tumor board had thoroughly reviewed Braelyn’s MRI.

They were amazed.

There is NO VISIBLE TUMOR.

Even the ~10% Dr. Liau had to leave behind during surgery because of its intimate involvement with critical structures is no longer visible.

She emphasized how amazed and pleased the entire tumor board was by such a complete response at this point.

Her assessment: the prior radiation and the ongoing DCVax appear to be working very well.

Their recommendation after also reviewing the Keytruda regimen Braelyn recently started?

KEEP DOING WHAT SHE’S DOING.

😭🙏

First and foremost, we give ALL thanks and glory to God.

People all over the world have prayed for this girl. I cannot begin to express how humbled and grateful we are.

But tonight I also cannot stop thinking about how close Braelyn came to never having this opportunity.

Earlier this year, her tumor was enormous and growing rapidly.

We sought help from multiple surgeons—including at prestigious institutions.

We were told further surgery was too risky.

We were offered the same old options: chemotherapy and photon radiation that would affect most of her brain, given the size of her tumor. 

Her tumor is MGMT-unmethylated, so for Braelyn, chemo was all risk with little to no benefit. 

And then a stranger I met here on X changed everything. @ThomasOwenMcCa1 connected us with Dr. Liau.

After reviewing Braelyn’s case, one of the first things she said was:

“This girl needs surgery right away.”

I told her we knew that. We just couldn’t find anyone willing to do it.

I asked if SHE would.

“If you can get her to me, I will do her surgery.”

We got Braelyn to UCLA.

Within two weeks, Dr. Liau operated and removed ~90% of a massive tumor spanning three lobes, stopping where continuing would risk critical structures.

And this time, her tumor tissue was PROPERLY PRESERVED.

That tissue was ultimately sent to England and used to manufacture Braelyn’s personalized DCVax vaccine.

She has now received 3 induction doses + her first booster.

And today?

The tumor that Dr. Liau had to leave behind is no longer visible on MRI.

Think about that.

And then think about what could have happened if we had simply accepted “there’s nothing else we can do.”

THIS is why I will not stop advocating for reform.

Patients should not have to find potentially life-saving treatment options accidentally through strangers on social media.

Patients should be told about legitimate investigational options when standard treatment offers little hope.

Patients undergoing tumor surgery should be informed BEFORE surgery about preservation of tissue that could potentially be used for personalized treatments.

And patients should have the right to make informed decisions about which risks they are willing to take.

Promising science means very little if the patients who need it cannot access it.

Braelyn is living proof of why access matters.

Tonight, though, advocacy can wait for just a moment.

Tonight I’m her mom.

And I finally get to say the words I have begged God to someday let me say:

NO EVIDENCE OF DISEASE.

Thank You, God.

Thank you, Dr. Liau.

Thank you to everyone who opened a door, donated, shared her story, fought for her and prayed for our girl.

There is always light, even in the darkest places.

Tonight that light is shining incredibly bright. ❤️🙏

#DCVaxForBraelyn #CureNotCovered

Global News Brief  
1. ESPN: Caitlin Clark celebrated her first FIBA Women’s World Cup championship by sharing Team USA’s victory graphic on Instagram after the Americans defeated France 97–79. Clark scored 12 points on 4-of-5 shooting, added three assists and two three-pointers, and dribbled out the final seconds as Team USA secured its fifth consecutive and 12th overall World Cup gold medal.

2. Politico: The Supreme Court blocked the Trump administration from implementing new Postal Service requirements for mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections, leaving a lower-court injunction in place. The proposed system required states to submit voter lists and use approved barcoded envelopes, but critics warned that introducing it so close to the election could prevent millions of valid ballots from being delivered.

3. NY Times: Saudi Arabia shut down a critical oil pipeline after a drone attack launched from Iraqi territory, heightening fears of further supply disruptions and briefly pushing global oil prices to about $110 per barrel.

4. WARSAW, Poland (AP): Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia may intensify provocations at Ukraine’s border crossings with European countries after Russian drones reportedly killed two people at the Ukraine Moldova border and a separate threat to a Polish Ukrainian crossing was averted. Tusk offered no details or evidence linking Russia to the Polish incident but said CIA Director Jim Ratcliffe had briefed him on heightened regional risks in the coming months.

5. The 10-Point: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has urged the AI industry to slow the development of advanced systems, receiving support from Sam Altman and Elon Musk, yet Anthropic has not slowed its own work. The contradiction highlights the company’s central moral conflict: although founded partly over concerns about OpenAI’s approach to safety and despite warnings from its employees about potentially dangerous technology, Anthropic remains locked in the race to develop the most powerful AI first.

6. Financial Times: A flood of ultra-cheap Chinese solar panels—now costing about 12 cents per watt—is driving rapid adoption by households and businesses worldwide, particularly in countries such as Pakistan, India, South Africa and the Philippines. The boom is lowering energy costs and reducing dependence on traditional utilities, but it is also straining grids, disrupting utility revenues and raising concerns that poorer customers may shoulder more infrastructure costs, forcing power systems and tariffs to adapt quickly to decentralized generation.

7. The Guardian: A California geomorphologist discovered an exceptionally well-preserved, roughly 10,000-year-old Pacific mastodon molar in a San Mateo County nature preserve after initially mistaking it for a rock. Experts called it the region’s most complete mastodon tooth, and it has been donated to Stanford University for carbon dating and research into Ice Age ecosystems and biodiversity.

8. Financial Times: A consortium led by Michael Dell’s family office, DFO Management, and Sequence Holdings is nearing a $7.7 billion deal to take insurance broker The Baldwin Group private. The acquisition, which could be announced as soon as Monday, comes amid a broader wave of consolidation in the insurance brokerage industry.

9. Just The News: German prosecutors allege that Hamas planned coordinated terrorist attacks against Israeli and Jewish targets in Berlin and Vienna to coincide with the second anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks on Israel, with the plots intended to unfold simultaneously or in close succession.

10. Daily News: Actress, Jean Smart made Emmy history by becoming the first woman to win for every season of her show, earning her fifth consecutive Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series award for “Hacks.”

11. Politico: Italy is moving closer to reviving nuclear power after nearly four decades, with the Senate advancing legislation establishing rules for new-generation reactors. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government is focusing on small modular reactors, with the first potentially operating by 2035, to strengthen energy security, reduce imports and emissions, and complement renewable power—despite continuing political and public opposition.

12. Financial Times: The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield reached 5% for the first time since 2023 as surging oil prices fueled inflation concerns and triggered a broad sell-off in global government bonds.

13.  The Guardian: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said a Russian drone strike on a passenger train near Ukraine’s border with Poland would not weaken Western support for Kyiv. The train was hit shortly after a convoy carrying senior diplomats and former leaders, including Boris Johnson and David Petraeus, passed through, prompting condemnation from European leaders.

14.  Politico: Sweden’s election remained too close to call with 95% of votes counted, as Magdalena Andersson’s center-left bloc held a three-seat lead over Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing alliance in the 349-member parliament. Final results may not be known until Wednesday, while both leaders begin negotiations to assemble a governing majority.

15. ESPN: The Giants opened their season with a 28–20 victory over the Cowboys, led by Jaxson Dart’s three touchdown passes and Isaiah Likely’s two touchdown catches. The Jets also began 1–0, defeating the Titans 23–10 behind Geno Smith’s efficient passing and Breece Hall’s 102 rushing yards and a touchdown.

16. CNBC: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged the AI industry to deliberately slow the development of increasingly powerful systems, warning that advances are outpacing safeguards. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk endorsed the call, with Altman pledging to give independent evaluators extensive access to OpenAI, while emphasizing that “pacing” development means improving oversight and safety—not stopping progress.

text:
THE VOICES

Gibney interviewed Musk's first wife Justine Musk, Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard, neurologist Sam Harris, tech reporter Kara Swisher, former USAID administrator Samantha Power, and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton . The most-discussed interview is with Ashley St. Clair, a former MAGA influencer who shares a child with Musk. She alleges that after the birth of their son, Musk offered her $40 million to sign a non-disclosure agreement and not speak in the film. "I want to give my children the example that we should never allow being materially comfortable to prevent us from telling the truth," she said at Venice . Musk denied the claim on X, calling it false .

THE AI AVATAR

Musk refused to participate in the documentary and sent Gibney a legal threat instead . Gibney's solution was unconventional: the film uses a CGI avatar of Musk, voice-synced to things Musk has actually said, based on a database of his existing clips . Gibney said the choice was intentionally ironic, referencing Musk's belief in simulation theory and meant to convey "the reality of what he's done and the unreality of his narrative" .

THE LEGAL RESPONSE

Musk's attorney Alex Spiro sent a letter to Gibney and Jigsaw Productions after the Venice premiere, accusing the documentary of misrepresenting facts and threatening legal action . Musk himself called it a "hit piece," "boring," and Gibney "a horrible human" and "a bitter old man who lost the plot long ago" . At TIFF, Gibney responded: "I reached out immediately. But he clearly wasn't interested in talking. We made so many formal outreaches to him, and with the exception of his remarks on Twitter, we received nothing back" . Jigsaw Productions defended the film's accuracy and invoked the First Amendment, noting that Musk "has proclaimed himself to be a free speech absolutist" .

THE RELEASE

The theatrical release was moved up from October 16 to October 9, in response to "overwhelming demand" . It will open in New York and Los Angeles before expanding nationwide. HBO Max holds streaming rights . Gibney also expressed concern about the film's streaming fate given the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery takeover battle, noting that Larry Ellison—cited in the film and an investor in Musk's Twitter acquisition—has a son, David Ellison, leading the Paramount side. "He'll twist whatever facts are at his disposal in order to please the head of state," Gibney said .

There are three important categories:

Closed Models
→ Weights and training details are not openly available.

Open-Weight Models
→ Model weights are available, but training data or the full training pipeline may not be.

The better question is:

text:
⭐️ Morgan Stanley

September 13, 2026

AI Infrastructure: The Materials Super-Cycle (Japan)

Global Materials

Our global materials team examines the upstream supply chains supporting the PCB and MLCC ecosystem. We focus on where AI-driven demand could reshape segment growth trajectories, capacity requirements, and competitive positioning.

-Key Takeaways

We see more attractive entry points in select upstream bottlenecks…
…than in parts of the downstream AI hardware chain, where expectations are already more demanding.

We think glass fabric, copper foil, resin, and optic fiber are most in shortage. We expect supply tightness to continue into 2028.

Our preferred stock exposures are Nittobo, Grace Fabric, Mitsui Kinzoku, Co-Tech, Corning, Furukawa Electric, Mitsubishi Gas Chemical, and Denka.
They have what we view as the cleanest earnings sensitivity to these bottlenecks.
 
⸻
 
The AI materials group has re-rated…

This group comprises the listed upstream suppliers of key materials across the PCB/CCL, AIDC, and broader AI value chains covered in this report.

It is up 91% over the past 12 months. However, as of September 10, 2026, it has corrected ~36% from its 52-week high in May–June 2026.

…but we do not think all of the opportunity is priced in:

Importantly, despite the robust rally over the past 12 months, based on our estimates, 2026 P/E for the AI materials group is ~26x, vs. ~33x for PCB/CCL.

Both are part of the same AI/data center infrastructure trade.
We see AI/data center PCB and CCL demand growing >6x and >7x, respectively, by 2030.

This means stronger demand for upstream materials — and scope for the valuation gap with PCB/CCL peers to narrow.
 
⸻
 
Segment ranking – high-end glass fabric #1, HVLP4+ copper foil #2, optical fiber #3
For #1 and #2, supply can’t respond quickly enough to accelerating AI demand; we see the strongest combination of scarcity, pricing power, and earnings leverage into 2027.

Fundamentals for #3 remain strong, but announced capacity additions make medium-term risk/reward less compelling.
 
⸻
 
CCL still a core preference #4:
AI/data center CCL demand up >7x by 2030.
Grade migration (M8 → M9/M10) helps sustain volume and product mix growth.
 
⸻
 
Resins — intact structural growth, less scarcity:
Volume growth and product mix upgrades offer support.
Less acute supply tightness limits near-term pricing upside.
 
⸻
 
Synthetic diamonds, tungsten, and molybdenum still offer longer-duration optionality
— hinging on technology adoption and material substitution.
 
⸻
 
Morgan Stanley conclusion
Greater China Materials — Asia Pacific Industry View: Attractive

text:
He Thought Statues and Icons Were Idolatry—Then Sam Shamoun Opened the Bible - More Sam Shamoun

Are Catholic statues and icons a form of idolatry—and does the Bible prohibit Christians from venerating sacred images? In this powerful discussion, Sam Shamoun responds to a young Catholic who was raised around Protestant objections and fears that honoring Catholic statues, icons, the Virgin Mary, and the saints might cross the line into worship.

Sam Shamoun explains the crucial biblical difference between veneration and idolatry. Idolatry occurs when someone treats a creature as a god or goddess and offers that creature the worship belonging exclusively to the Creator. Catholics and Eastern Orthodox Christians do not believe that Mary, Paul, Michael, the angels, or the saints are gods. Honoring an image of a saint is therefore not the same as worshipping that saint as God.

Opening Exodus 20 and Romans 1:21–25, Sam Shamoun examines what Scripture actually condemns. The Bible condemns rejecting God, worshipping creation instead of the Creator, and transforming created beings into false gods. Sam Shamoun argues that these passages cannot be interpreted as a universal prohibition against every religious image, because God Himself commanded Moses to make golden cherubim for the Ark of the Covenant in Exodus 25 and Exodus 37. Sacred images also appeared throughout Solomon’s Temple.

Sam Shamoun then discusses the bronze serpent, explaining that the image became sinful only when the Israelites began treating it as a god. The same distinction appears when Joshua and the elders bow before the Ark of the Covenant without worshipping the cherubim as gods. The conversation ultimately addresses Catholic veneration, Protestant objections to icons, the Virgin Mary, the saints, the Ten Commandments, the Eucharist, biblical worship, the Ark of the Covenant, and the difference between honoring a sacred image and committing idolatry.

text:
I don't think the latter holds up textually.  The entire thrust of the prophetic picture that we've been discussing thus far in terms of atonement is about the shedding of innocent blood being sufficient to cleanse and prepare the way for approach to the throne of God.

In that context we're told that “Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.” (Eph. 5:2), which is very much Christ the Son offering Himself in temple language.  So Hebrews 7 says that Jesus accomplished salvation "once for all when He offered up Himself" - not to human violence, but to the One to whom all worship is due (hence the fragrant offering - seen even in the typified gold, frankincense and myrrh: Gold for a king, frankincense for God, and myrrh for burial).

I don't think Jesus willingly laying down His life (even through violence) and offering Himself up, submitting to the will of the Father for the redemption of man, are necessarily conflicting propositions.  The Scriptures clearly discuss both.

So if your argument here is "man desired and perpetrated the violence, therefore Christ wasn't a sacrifice offered to God", then that's a place I can't follow you to - as the text explicitly states otherwise.

But I think the point that...  those who crucified Jesus did indeed desire this violence, but that Jesus nonetheless made Himself perfect through obedience to the Father - even through the death on the cross - makes His willing sacrificial life and death an offering on behalf of those He loved unto God.

So man has a role to play there.  In some kind of twisted way, the violence of man was in fact producing an offering of sorts through the faithfulness of the Son. Jesus was crucified, just as the lambs were slain in the temple... Our violence was ultimately part of the mechanism that brought us peace. "The punishment that brought us peace was upon Him".

But that's still not an either/or proposition.

text:
Reminds me of this 🤪

During the COVID-19 pandemic, sports teams across the globe used cardboard cutouts of fans, pets, and mascots to fill empty stadium seats, creating a visual sense of normalcy for television broadcasts and players.  This trend emerged after leagues forced games to be played in empty arenas due to health restrictions.

Teams offered these cutouts as paid fan experiences or fundraising opportunities, with prices varying by organization.  For example, UNLV sold cutouts for $79, Bradley University for $75, and UCSB for $50, with proceeds often directed to scholarship funds or charitable causes like Blues for Kids. Some teams, such as the Los Angeles Dodgers, used cutouts of celebrities and former players, while the Denver Broncos famously displayed 1,800 cardboard cutouts of the entire cast of South Park in their stadium.

The cutouts served multiple purposes beyond aesthetics: they helped maintain physical distancing between limited groups of allowed attendees (such as the 30,000 cutouts used at the 2021 Super Bowl) and provided emotional support for athletes.  At Bradley University, players' families and friends were featured in the stands, allowing players to take selfies with their loved ones' cutouts after games. In some cases, the cutouts became part of the game action itself, such as when a home run nearly decapitated a Dodgers cutout during an exhibition game.

text:
Tonight, Kenneth Walker III ran for a career-high 173 yards and scored two touchdowns, one on the ground and one through the air, in his debut for the Kansas City Chiefs.

Eight years ago, doctors told him he would never play football again.

In the summer of 2018, Walker was a high school kid in Tennessee with a dream and no Power Five offers. He was grinding before his senior season, the way he always had, certain this was the year he'd finally break through and force college coaches to notice him.

Then one morning he woke up and couldn't breathe.

His mother rushed him to the hospital. Doctors found blood clots in his lungs, a pulmonary embolism, a condition that can turn fatal fast. They shut him down from all sports immediately. And then they told a teenager chasing a football dream the worst thing he could hear: that if he'd taken a hit in the wrong place while playing through that chest pain, it could have killed him.

Football was over. That was the diagnosis. In an instant, the dream was gone.

Walker refused to accept it as the ending.

With treatment, time, and his family behind him, he fought his way back onto the field. He had no scholarship offers from major programs even then, so he started at Wake Forest, transferred to Michigan State, and in one unforgettable 2021 season ran for over 1,600 yards and became one of the most electric backs in the country. The Seattle Seahawks made him a second-round pick in 2022.

For three years he was good, but stuck in a committee, splitting carries, waiting for a real shot to carry a team.

This past February, he got it. Walker carried Seattle through the playoffs, then rushed for 135 yards in Super Bowl LX and was named the game's Most Valuable Player. Months later he signed a big free-agent deal to become the every-down back in Kansas City.

Tonight, in his first game in a Chiefs uniform, he was everything they paid for. He ran for 173 yards, the most of his entire career, including a 60-yard touchdown burst where he hit better than 21 miles per hour, one of the fastest runs he's ever broken off. He added a touchdown catch for good measure, and the Chiefs rolled to a win over the Broncos.

Not bad for a kid who was once told, by doctors, that he'd already played his last down.

text:
Ms. Parker’s AFR anniversary piece treats AUKUS’s survival through leadership churn as a headline-making strategic achievement.  

This is a wrongful categorization: endurance through two Australian PMs, two US presidents and five British PMs is not proof of strategic quality.  It is proof only that the two major Australian parties locked the country into a multi-decade, multi-hundred-billion commitment with no parliamentary contest.  Labor adopted Morrison’s deal overnight; the Coalition still treats it as sacred while opposition from The Greens, @DavidShoebridge, Keating, Evans, Husic and parts of the Labor rank-and-file are treated as background noise.  

That is uniparty lock-in, not democratic resilience: a junior middle-power partner is writing large, multi-decade cheques into the US and UK military-industrial bases, building docks and workforce pipelines that primarily service allied boats, and accepting second-hand platforms with no binding guarantee of transfer.  Sovereignty language in the communiqués does not change the substantive industrial or legal reality: the president of the day decides whether any Virginia class submarine leaves US inventory.  Australia's strategic investment is perpetual vassal-state tributary behaviour dressed up as “optimal pathway.”  

A strong navy may be a serious Australian interest.  However, paying hundreds of billions for a naval capability that 1) arrives long after the operational window its own advocates keep naming, 2) is dependent on partners who cannot currently build enough boats for themselves, 3) while converting national infrastructure into a forward node for someone else’s fleet, is not serious strategy.  It is an expensive way to confuse political continuity with national interest.  

The industrial facts are worse than the politics: the UK cannot manufacture attack submarines at the rate or reliability AUKUS assumes.  Parliamentary inquiry after inquiry has found funding shortfalls, “critically low” availability and a yard at Barrow that takes more than a decade per boat.  HMS Anson’s visit to Australia was cut short when the Royal Navy needed the only boat it had at sea.  Promising Australia a new SSN-AUKUS class from that base is heroic optimism, not a plan worthy of even being considered strategic.  The United States is not going to sell Australia new Virginia-class boats on the original timetable.  Congress and the Pentagon have already shifted the offer to three in-service boats.  Even those transfers require a sitting president to certify that handing them over will not weaken the US Navy, itself already well short of its own force-level goal.  Billions of Australian money have gone into US yards without lifting the production rate.  That is not a delivery schedule, it is a hope that Washington will one day feel rich enough in hulls to spare a few used ones.

But the timing is the real killer.  Hegseth, Rudd and the Washington-Canberra commentariat have spent years pointing at 2027–28 as the elevated-risk window over Taiwan - Xi’s fourth term, Taiwan’s election cycle, the deterrence calculation.  The first Australian-owned Virginia is still spoken of for 2032.  The first Australian-built SSN-AUKUS sits in the early 2040s, if the UK industrial base and Adelaide workforce both perform miracles.  

What Australia actually gets in the advertised danger years is a US/UK rotational presence at Stirling from late 2027 as a de facto permanent US base on AU soil, and a growing maintenance hub at Henderson.  That is American operating infrastructure on Australian soil, paid for by Australian taxpayers and, via Force Posture, chain-of-command controlled by the US military's strategic interests in positioning AU as the epicenter of US power projection in the Indo-Pacific.   It is not even an Australian fleet, let alone a world-class Navy, that can independently handle the looming crisis of the US' own manufacture.

Ms. Parker describes this in the article cited below as "a persistent... feature of Australian strategic thinking".  Indeed: yet more's the pity as such is also a regrettably self-evident indictment of any "Australian strategic thinking" ability beyond subordination to US war policy out of willfully blind faith that ANZUS and the AU/US alliance is sacrosanct and AUKUS is therefore invulnerable.

text:
SNAP-ON $SNA LENDS MECHANICS THE MONEY TO BUY ITS OWN TOOLBOXES:

The Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 is watching Snap-on at $377.78, +$2.34 / +0.62% from Friday's $375.44 close, first of fifty-one. The Kenosha, Wisconsin company, 13,000 employees, founded 1920, makes the wrenches, diagnostic scanners and rolling tool chests that mechanics buy from a franchisee who drives a van to their shop.

The verdict: the business is durable and the price is genuinely low, but the figure that settles this is not a tool figure. A fifth of Snap-on's operating profit comes from lending, and last quarter it lent less.

The lending is the part most people miss. A mechanic buys tools on an installment plan running about four years, and Snap-on writes that loan itself rather than sending them to a bank. It carries $1.87B of those loans plus $532M owed by shops on larger equipment - about $2.4B of credit out the door from a $19.5B company.

What that arm earns, from the July 23 report for the three months to July 4:

- Financial Services revenue $99.7M; operating earnings $67.5M - 68 cents of profit on every revenue dollar
- The three tool divisions earned $268.9M between them, so lending is 20% of all operating profit
- It out-earned the entire Commercial and Industrial division, which made $66.5M on $395.8M of sales

Now the figure that is slipping: new credit written in the quarter was $281.0M, down 4.1%, with that arm's earnings easing to $67.5M from $68.2M. It is the only line here going backwards, and the one that tracks how confident a mechanic feels about four years of work ahead.

The tools sold fine. Net sales $1,235.1M, +4.7%, organic sales - growth once purchases and currency moves come out - +3.0%. Gross margin, what survives of each sales dollar after the cost of making the product, 51.4% against 50.5%. Net earnings $260.6M, $4.96 a diluted share against $4.72 - 21 cents of every sales dollar kept. Commercial and Industrial margin reached 16.8%, up 3.3 points and its best ever.

One name, six Len5es:

- DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - STRONG, and the Len5 watching it, first of fifty-one. Wants settled earning power bought cheaply while giving no credit for money in the bank. Settled is not arguable: it has earned between $4.51 and $4.96 a share in every one of the last seven quarters. Cheap is 19.2 times the last year of profit. And refusing to count the balance sheet still leaves $1,644.7M of cash against $1,204.0M of debt. CHANGE IT: bad-debt charges rising while originations keep falling, turning settled earning power into a credit question.

- QUALITY-VALUE - STRONG, fourth of fifty-four. Wants a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought under what it is worth. The unbuildable part is not the wrench. It is a franchisee who parks outside the same shop every week and already holds that mechanic's four-year payment plan - a rival can copy the tool, not the relationship or the loan book. Fourth rather than first is the price: 3.21 times book value - what owners would keep after selling everything and paying every debt - is a narrow discount. CHANGE IT: gross margin falling back under 50% while that multiple holds.

- INCOME - PARTIAL. Wants cash reaching owners that the business itself funds. Funding is emphatic: six months sent $253.2M out in dividends and $191.3M in buybacks, $444.5M against roughly $596M of free cash flow - the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment. Size holds it back: $2.44 a quarter, $9.76 a year, about 2.6% here, ex-dividend August 19 and paid September 10. CHANGE IT: the payment rising toward the cash that covers it, rather than taking about 42 cents of it.

- GROWTH - NOT A FIT. Wants profit growth the price has not already charged for. The price charges almost nothing; the growth is the objection. Profit per share rose 5.1% and organic sales 3.0% - steady, not growing. The two businesses bought this year, Hi-Force Hydraulic Tools and Diesel Laptops, added $11.5M of sales, under 1% of the quarter. CHANGE IT: organic sales reaching a high-single-digit pace, which needs the van business to do better than 3%.

- MOMENTUM - NOT A FIT. Wants a price near the top of its one-year range with the recent climb and the longer one agreeing. Neither holds: $377.78 sits 10.7% under the $423.02 of August 6 and only 17.8% above the $320.80 low of November 18 last year. CHANGE IT: a close back above $423.02.

- HYPERGROWTH - NOT A FIT, and furthest off. Wants a business early as well as fast. Founded 1920, sales growing 3%. CHANGE IT: nothing on this company's calendar.

Stanley Black & Decker at $88.89, -$0.35 / -0.39% today, is what that van is worth. The New Britain, Connecticut company, 43,500 employees, makes the DeWalt and Craftsman tools sold to whoever walks into a hardware store, and books no loan when they do. Same quarter, ended the same day: revenue $3,960.7M - 3.2 times Snap-on's - and net income $351.3M, keeping 8.9 cents of each sales dollar against Snap-on's 21.1. A real recovery from $101.9M a year ago. It fits none of the six Len5es: at 21.8 times profit on those thinner margins, neither value Len5 is offered a discount.

WATCH originations, not sales. The sales line says whether mechanics are buying. Originations say whether they will sign for four more years. WHEN: third-quarter results are tentatively Thursday, October 15, before the open, with $4.96 a share carried - exactly what it just earned. RISK: $2.4B lent to individual tradespeople is a bank's risk sitting inside a tool company, though it is not deteriorating yet - six-month bad-debt provisions on those loans ran $35.6M against $36.5M a year earlier.

A mechanic signing one of these plans this month is betting on their own workload into 2030. Snap-on was asked to make that bet 4.1% less often last quarter, and it is the first of its numbers to move.

text:
FLYWIRE CORPORATION $FLYW - 13-STEP ANALYSIS
After a discussion with @realroseceline I decided to run Flywire through Buffett's 13-step framework, continuing my search for a company which I believe can generate a 20% pre-tax compounded annual rate of return over the next five years. 

TLDR: Based on management guidance regarding revenue growth, EBITDA margin expansion, share count flattening and SBC as a % of revenue falling, I believe that an investment in Flywire as of market close on Friday, September 11th can compound at over 22% through January 2031. There are some aspects of Flywire's business I really like, including: (i) consistent earnings growth since going public in 2021, albeit from a negative base; (ii) strategic acquisitions by management; (iii) the absence of leverage; and (iv) a lack of capital intensity required to maintain operations. However, given that 25% of my portfolio is allocated to dLocal, I am hesitant to add another payments company and am taking a pass on Flywire for now. 

Step One: What does Flywire Do?
Flywire is a global software and payments company that aims to simplify large, complex, and cross-border transactions for institutions and businesses. 77% of company revenue comes from processing post-secondary education tuition payments. The remaining 23% of company revenue comes from facilitating: (i) international luxury bookings and hotel event payments [13% of revenue]; (ii) patient billing at hospitals [7% of revenue]; and (iii) invoice-to-cash workflows for B2B transactions [3% of revenue].

Flywire generates ~80% of its revenue via a take rate on total payment volume processed. On cross-border transactions, Flywire derives this take rate through: (i) payment processing fees; and (ii) FX spreads, whereby the company receives local currency from the payor and quotes them at a FX rate ~150-200bps above the official FX rate Flywire later uses. On domestic transactions Flywire earns a lower average monetization rate, as there is no FX conversion to gain a spread on and payment processing fees are diluted by interchange and network fees owed to the payor’s bank and card network. Overall, Flywire’s blended take rate on $37.6B of total payment volume in FY2025 was 1.34%, down from 1.38% on $29.7B of TPV in FY2024.

The remaining 20% of company revenue is generated via subscriptions to its various platforms, including: (i) StudyLink, which assists university staff in reviewing student applications; (ii) tuition payment plans and past-due tuition recovery for university staff dealing with delinquent payments; (iii) patient payment plans and billing communications for hospital staff to manage patients unable to pay their medical bills; and (iv) Sertifi, which Flywire bought for $330M in February 2025 and simplifies the process whereby institutions book and pay for events at international and domestic hotels. Platform and other revenue reached $120.4M in FY2025, up 47% YoY vs 22.5% YoY growth in transaction revenue.

To illustrate the value Flywire adds for its customers, consider the following transaction between Raj, an Indian national going to college in the US, and Ohio State, the post-secondary institution which Raj is attending. In the absence of Flywire, Raj’s $60 thousand tuition payment has to travel through a chain of banks that do have relationships with each other before eventually reaching Ohio State’s bank.

There are a number of problems with Raj’s payment flowing through a stream of banks:
• Raj’s local bank in Mumbai charges him an FX rate to convert his rupee payment into USD which is: (i) 300-400bps higher the rupee-dollar rate available to the bank’s institutional clients; and (ii) 100-200bps higher than the FX rate charged by Flywire. On Raj’s $60 thousand payment, a 3-4% FX conversion fee contributes another $2 thousand.

• Each intermediary bank takes a small wire fee, reducing the tuition payment sent to Ohio State such that Raj may not have paid his tuition in full.

• The payment flow from Raj’s local bank to Ohio State’s bank can take three-to-five business days with no tracking optionality by either Raj or Ohio State.

• The short text field documenting the purpose of the payment, sender and recipient often becomes truncated as it passes between each bank, introducing the risk that Ohio State will not recognize the payment when it arrives in their bank account, especially if there are multiple individuals with the same name and no student ID is provided on the transfer.

• Raj’s local government may limit how much money he can send abroad each year or require the completion of specific forms to send his $60 thousand payment internationally. If Raj fills out this form incorrectly, his bank would refuse to send the transfer and he may not discover this error for days, delaying his tuition payment to Ohio State.

For Ohio State, a late, unidentifiable or insufficient payment would cause them to impose sanctions on Raj, including late fees or a ban on course registration.

With Ohio State as a Flywire customer, tuition-payment complexity is simplified in the following manner:
• Raj goes to the Ohio State’s website, clicks "pay tuition," and is diverted to the Flywire site, which recognizes he is in India and displays payment options in rupees including: (i) net banking; (ii) unified payments interface (“UPI”); (iii) local bank transfer; and (iv) Indian debit card.

• Raj picks a payment method and transfers his money to a domestic Indian bank account owned by Flywire with no wire form, SWIFT code or intermediary banks. The payment owing, $60,804 to reflect Flywire’s 1.34% take rate, is fixed, removing the risk that hidden fees will cause Raj’s tuition payment to be insufficient.

• Despite having to pay a 1.34% premium for Flywire’s services, on a net basis Raj saves ~2%, or $1,200, on FX fees by using Flywire instead of his local bank. This is because, with Flywire, Raj’s rupee-denominated payment is transferred to the company's Indian bank account. The US$60 thousand which Flywire sends to Ohio State comes from Flywire’s US bank account, and the company squares up its own positions in bulk, later, at a wholesale exchange rate.

• Raj is provided with a tracking page and email updates when his payment is received, converted, sent and delivered. A Flywire helpline which speaks in Raj’s local language is also provided and open 24/7. Further, Flywire’s client-facing dashboard for Ohio State’s finance staff lists every payment coming in, who sent it, which student it belongs to, and its status. Via this dashboard, Ohio State’s finance team can search, run reports, issue a refund with a click instead of arranging an outbound wire, and see a payment that's still in transit rather than wondering about its status.

• When Raj’s payment arrives at Ohio State, it is tagged with his student ID, full name, and purpose. The payment is integrated directly into Workday, Ohio State’s student database platform, so that Raj’s balance updates automatically and he is cleared to register for clients.

Step Two: Is Flywire a Consumer Monopoly?
No. I will explain why below.

The argument can be made that Flywire is a type three consumer monopoly, as it provides a repetitive service that: (i) businesses and consumers are constantly in need of; and (ii) is not capital intensive to deliver. The repetitive nature of the transactions which Flywire facilitates is illustrated by the company’s customer stickiness data, with management reporting <1% revenue churn of enterprise clients in FY2025 and net dollar-based retention of ~114% in FY2024.

Further, Flywire has a three-part moat which raises barriers to entry for competition, including the: (i) complexity; and (ii) size of the transactions it facilitates; and (iii) lock-in effect associated with the integration of Flywire's software into client platforms.

On complexity, Flywire holds payor funds before remitting them, which makes it a money transmitter and requires licensing in every jurisdiction the company operates in. Each licence carries capital requirements, mandates the segregation of client funds and imposes anti-money-laundering obligations, while Flywire must also collect whatever documentation the payor's local government demands before their money can leave the country. The burden of satisfying these requirements for Flywire is fixed by jurisdiction. For example, the licensing fees and human capital devoted to obtaining a licence to operate in France do not scale with the total payment volume Flywire processes in France. With the company now serving over 240 countries and territories across the world, Flywire has already expended significant resources attaining the necessary licences and can spread these regulatory costs across all of its payment volume. A new entrant must incur the same cost over a multi-year approval timeline without the volume in other jurisdictions to absorb it, representing a barrier of both capital and time.

On transaction size, for the large-ticket payments Flywire facilitates both merchants and payors are incentivized toward bank transfers rather than credit cards, insulating the business from card-based competition such as Ayden and Stripe. For merchants, willingness to absorb a 2.5% card fee falls as transaction size rises. Where merchants impose a surcharge on a large-ticket transaction to recover the cost of a 2.5% card fee, payors overwhelmingly elect bank transfer instead. Even without a surcharge, making such a large purchase on credit is inherently risky, carries significant interest, and for those with low credit limits is impossible. Cards were engineered for small, frequent, low-risk retail purchases, not the large-ticket purchases which Flywire facilitates.

While complexity, transaction size and Flywire’s software attachment all deter new entrants, Flywire faces meaningful competition from established corridor specialists including Convera, PayMyTuition and TransferMate. Because each of these incumbents offers essentially the same service as Flywire, competition occurs based on price. For example, institutions such as Colgate University list each of Convera, PayMyTuition and Flywire on their student accounts platform as concurrent international payment options. To a student paying their tuition, the most important factor when choosing which company should process their payment will be the FX rate offered. On these grounds, it is fair to conclude that Flywire is a price taker and not a consumer monopoly.

As a price taker, Flywire's profitability faces the following headwinds, with one prospective and the other already underway: (i) the public provision of payment infrastructure; and (ii) international student visa restrictions, which are shifting a growing share of TPV toward domestic transactions that carry no FX conversion and a materially lower take rate.

First, through the implementation of state-sponsored payment rails such as UPI in India and Pix in Brazil, domestic transfers are now instant and effectively free and are being extended into cross-border corridors. If individuals are able to use public rails to instantly transfer large sums of money internationally without FX fees, Flywire will need to lower the FX spread it charges payors. Importantly, this is a prospective, and potentially distant, risk.

The second headwind, international student visa restrictions, is already impacting Flywire. Specifically, tightened visa restrictions in Canada and Australia caused Flywire management to guide each market down ~20% YoY in 2025, with $FLYW getting cut in half as a result in February 2025. In Q1 2026, management expressly identified visa restrictions in Australia, Canada and the United States as affecting payment flows. The financial consequences are visible in Flywire’s gross margin, which compressed to 53.4% in Q2 2026 from 57.0% in Q2 2025. Further, payment processing services costs grew 35.4% in FY2025 against revenue growth of 26.6% as a result of an increase in domestic transactions carrying a lower average monetization rate.

Flywire is attempting to offset these headwinds by focusing on platform revenue, which grew 47.0% against transaction revenue growth of 22.5% in FY2025 and reached ~20% of total revenue for the first time. However, even without rapid platform revenue growth and falling take rates, Flywire will likely continue to grow gross profit and realize operating leverage given its relatively fixed cost base. Moreover, although headwinds (i) and (ii) are serious, Flywire’s actual rate compression was only 4bps YoY in FY2025 and through H1 2026 is tracking closely with 2024 and 2025.

Step Three: Is Flywire Conservatively Financed
Yes, the company is effectively debt-free. As of June 30, 2026, Flywire’s total debt is ~$1.5M against $282M in cash.

Step Four: Has Flywire's EPS Growth been Strong, Stable, and Upward-Trending?
Yes, although a full 10-year history is not available given that Flywire went public in 2021 and an EPS CAGR cannot be computed as profitability was only achieved in FY2024.

As seen in the attached table titled “Flywire FY2021-FY2026E EPS”, Flywire’s EPS improved each year between FY2021 and FY2025, with consensus calling for another increase in FY2026. Importantly, this earnings growth has not been a product of financial engineering, as diluted shares outstanding have risen ~84% between FY2021 and FY2025.

Revenue growth has been strong, compounding at 32.7% between FY2021 and FY2025. Although the pace of revenue growth has decelerated fairly linearly since FY2022, this is to be expected as Flywire’s business matures and each year is being compared to a higher base. Management is guiding for $1B in organic revenue “within the next few years”, which infers that revenue is expected to continue compounding at a solid rate in the near future.

Beyond revenue growth, Flywire has realized significant operating leverage since FY2021, with adjusted EBITDA compounding at a ~52% CAGR between FY2021 and FY2025. This is because the majority of Flywire's operating cost base is fixed with respect to payment volume, meaning that incremental gross profit converts to adjusted EBITDA at a very high rate once Flywire's fixed cost base is covered.

The important implication is that take rate compression and improving cash generation are not mutually exclusive. Because OpEx is largely fixed, what matters for cash flow is the absolute dollar growth in gross profit, not the rate earned per dollar of volume. Adjusted gross profit grew 19.0% in Q2 2026 even as net take rate fell from 1.27% to 1.09% YoY. Provided that volume growth outpaces spread compression, gross profit will continue to rise and each incremental dollar of gross profit will convert to cash at a high rate against a cost base that does not scale proportionally.

Step Five: Does Flywire Management Allocate Capital Within its Realm of Expertise?
Yes. 

Flywire requires very little capital to operate, as will be discussed further in step eight, and pays no dividend, so capital allocation has been devoted to acquisitions and share repurchases.

Flywire has made a series of acquisitions since going public in 2021, purchasing the following companies: (i) WPM Group, a U.K. education payments provider, for an undisclosed sum in December 2021; (ii) Cohort Go, an Australian education agent payments platform, for $32.8M in July 2022; (iii) StudyLink, an Australian international student admissions software business, for $38.8M in November 2023; (iv) Invoiced, a Texas-based B2B invoice-to-cash SaaS platform, for $55.0M in August 2024; and (v) Sertifi, a Chicago-based hospitality contracting, e-signature and card authorization platform, for $330M in February 2025.

Transactions (i)-(iv) were minor, collectively totalling ~$150M (below 12-month trailing free cash flow of ~$165M). Further, each occurred in a vertical which Flywire already served (eduction and healthcare), strengthening the argument that management was allocating capital within its realm of expertise. The Sertifi transaction is ~2.2x larger than the combined value of acquisitions (i)-(iv), but also falls under one of Flywire’s core verticals (travel). Given the aforementioned headwinds facing Flywire’s education segment and broader take rate, the decision to acquire Sertifi, a high-margin software attachment, is defensible, especially considering that: (i) the price paid was reasonable (6x revenue while growing revenue ~35% YoY in 2025); (ii) Sertifi's card authorization function is payments-adjacent, addressing the practice of hotels exchanging card details by emailed PDF; and (iii) Flywire was able to finance the acquisition without taking on excessive leverage.

Step Six: Has Flywire used Retained Earnings to Grow EPS?
This step is not applicable, as Flywire’s cumulative EPS between 2021 and 2025 is negative.

Step Seven: Does Flywire Generate an Above-Average RoE?
No. 12-month trailing RoE is ~4%. However, I do not view this as especially informative, as Flywire only became profitable in 2024 and net income is suppressed by ~$70M of non-cash stock-based compensation and ~$28M of amortization. On 12-month trailing free cash flow of ~$165M, Flywire’s RoE is ~20.7%, clearing Buffett’s threshold. I expect Flywire’s RoE to improve materially as earnings improve against a static equity base.

Step Eight: Does Flywire Require Significant CapEx or R&D to Maintain Operations?
No. Flywire’s 12-month trailing CapEx is ~$1M against revenue of $713.5M. Because the company has effectively no physical assets to maintain, free cash flow tracks operating cash flow nearly perfectly.

Notably, Flywire’s technology and development costs amounted to ~$70M in FY2025, representing 11.3% of revenue. A substantial portion of this expense involves maintenance for Flywire’s software applications and the costs involved with staying current on payment-linked regulatory burdens. However, even when accounting for these expenses, Flywire is not a business which requires significant funding to maintain its operations.

Overall, Flywire sits within my realm of confidence on the basis that: (i) I understand the business model; (ii) the company’s balance sheet is debt-free; (iii) capital intensity is negligible; (iv) a real moat exists via payment complexity and size; (v) management has allocated capital sensibly; and (vi) earnings, revenue and adjusted EBITDA have all improved in every year since listing. I am wary of Flywire’s lack of pricing power, but comforted by the fact that even with falling take rates Flywire should be able to compound revenue at a reasonable rate and realize operating leverage against its relatively fixed cost base.

Step Nine: What is Flywire’s Initial Rate of Return Relative to the Risk-Free Rate?
At Flywire’s share price of $17.87 as of market close on September 11, 2026, the company’s earnings yield is ~0.5% based on FY2025 EPS of ~$0.10. Against a 10-year treasury yielding close to 5%, Flywire’s initial rate of return is unattractive. However, steps 10-13 will demonstrate that management expects Flywire to grow into its ~170x FY2025 trailing P/E valuation quickly.

Steps 10-13: Flywire Financial Projections and Forecasted Rate of Return through 2030
On Flywire’s Q2 2026 call, management reiterated their target for $1B of organic revenue and a 30% adj EBITDA margin “within the next few years”. To determine when this target will likely be achieved, I looked into Flywire’s pace of revenue growth and adj EBITDA margin expansion since 2020.

On the revenue front, growth has decelerated fairly linearly from ~52% in 2021 to a forecasted ~20% in 2026. Assuming revenue growth decelerates further to ~16% in 2027 and levels out at ~15% in 2028, management’s $1B revenue target will be achieved in 2028. This seems reasonable to me, and because the target is organic, revenue excludes the impact of any acquisitions.

Next, Flywire’s adj EBITDA margin has expanded rapidly, up ~1800bps since 2022 based on a 23% adj EBITDA margin target in 2026. The pace of margin expansion has decelerated gently since 2023, and is guided to begin flattening in 2027. Here is the five year trajectory of adj EBITDA margin expansion: (i) 530bps YoY in 2023; (ii) 540bps YoY in 2024; (iii) 380bps YoY in 2025; (iv) a guided 340bps in 2026; and (v) a guided 200bps YoY in 2027 to 25%. Based on this decelerating path, I think it is reasonable to assume that Flywire will attain its adj EBITDA margin target in 2030, with 200bps of expansion annually between 2027 and 2029, and 100bps of expansion in 2030.

Extrapolating $1B in 2028 revenue to 2030 at a 15% CAGR yields $1.32B in 2030 revenue. At a 30% adj EBITDA margin this amounts to $397M in 2030 adj EBITDA. Again, this does not include the impact of any acquisitions, so the revenue estimate is likely low.

Next, I adjusted out SBC and payroll taxes, which have increased 2.4x from $31.2M in 2022 to $75M targeted in 2026. Despite this outright increase, SBC + payroll taxes as a percentage of revenue are guided to be 80bps lower at ~10.0% than in 2022. The pace of SBC growth also appears to be slowing, with SBC + payroll taxes up 12% YoY in 2025 and guided to increase only 1% in 2026, well below the 45% YoY growth in each of 2023 and 2024. I assume that SBC + payroll taxes will increase 5% annually between 2027 and 2030, becoming a $91M expense in 2030 and falling to ~7% of revenue. This assumption is supported by management statements that they intend to continue reducing SBC as a % of revenue below 10%.

Turning to depreciation, Flywire’s D&A comprises two components: (i) property and equipment, which includes capitalized internal-use software, carried on a five-year life; and (ii) amortization of acquired intangibles. I break down the first component into depreciation of physical assets (~$2.5M in 2025) and amortization of capitalized software (~$3.5M), forecasting that these increase to ~$4M and ~$8M respectively by 2030. For the second component, I assume that amortization of acquired intangibles remains constant at $22M (as I did not account for the impact of any acquisitions in revenue). Overall, D&A lands at $34M in 2030.

With these forecasts in mind, and assuming that restructuring costs + FX are offset by interest income, my estimated 2030 pre-tax income for Flywire is $272M ($397M in adj EBITDA - $91M in SBC & payroll taxes - $34M in D&A). Using a 25% tax rate, this brings 2030 GAAP net income to $204M.

On Flywire’s Q2 2026 earnings call, management targeted FCF conversion at 70-75% of adj EBITDA. Using a 72% conversion rate, I expect Flywire’s FCF to be $286M in 2030, a 23.4% CAGR from 2026’s $124M estimate. From here, I assume that management will use 60% of FCF for buybacks given their intention to keep net dilution at a maximum of 3% annually. At an average conversion price of $28 a share and $949M of cumulative FCF between Sep 2026 and Jan 2031, I forecast that management will retire ~20M shares during this period against ~16M shares issued at an effective price of $23 via $363M of cumulative SBC. Using these assumptions, Flywire’s diluted shares outstanding will decrease from ~122M currently to ~118M in 2030, yielding $1.73 in 2030 EPS.

At a 25x multiple of 2030 forecasted EPS, Flywire's share price comes out to $43.25, a 22.6% CAGR based on a closing share price of $17.87 and a 4.33 year time horizon. I view a 25x multiple of GAAP earnings as defensible given forecasted revenue growth of 15% with 30% EBITDA margins and no meaningful debt. The impact of acquisitions is not included, and will likely push FLYW’s rate of return higher.

text:
Kerala is trending this week, so let me offer a comparison nobody asked for.
I have spent my whole life in Gujarat. I am still afraid of its breakfast.
Everything here arrives fried. Find a proper meal while travelling, and you must hunt down a food park.
Those food parks serve sambhar and chutney with great confidence. The confidence rarely survives your stomach for minutes.
Kerala does breakfast differently. Every small eatery, even in the remotest corner, manages to be both hygienic and proper. I do not mean the big chains everyone already knows. I mean the tiny places with no signboard worth mentioning.
Roads tell a similar story. Kerala's roads are narrow, but they are laid with real intent. Asphalt reaches almost every home, in almost every direction.
Leave the cities out of this — Kochi's roads deserve a sad column of their own. Rural Kerala, though, quietly outperforms most of urban India.
Gujarat has no such ambition. Outside the highways, roads seem designed for tractors, not cars. Nobody complains. Everyone has simply adjusted, the way Gujaratis adjust to most things.
There is more.
If you are a Malayali living in Kerala, social life finds you whether you seek it or not. Deaths, baptisms, weddings — the calendar is always full, and everyone is invited.
These gatherings are where you meet your relatives. Everywhere else, you mostly meet your friends, and quietly agree that this counts as family enough.
I will not dwell on the clean air, the water, the hills, the wildlife. That list writes itself.
What I will mention is the weekend. Kerala offers enough recreational spots to leave in the morning and return the same night, tired but satisfied. Wherever you are.
Gujarat has the longest coastline in the country and treats it like a liability. Thirteen hundred kilometres of coast, and not one proper seafood joint along the way.
A state with that much shoreline choosing to ignore its own fish is a mystery I have stopped trying to solve.
Till about a decade back, I thought Gujarat is my home state. That changed slowly. No offence to Gujarat though.

text:
The premise assumes the war turned on which way the panzers pointed. It didn't, and we actually have the experiment already run for us.

Start with August 1941. Halder, chief of the Army General Staff, fought hard to keep driving on Moscow. Guderian backed him at first. Then Guderian went into a private meeting with Hitler, no Halder present, and came out having dropped the argument entirely and agreed to swing his panzer group south. 

The result was the Kiev encirclement. German figures put Red Army prisoners as high as two thirds of a million, though the German high command was never a trustworthy source on such numbers. What isn't disputed is that the detour burned five or six irreplaceable weeks and shoved the Moscow offensive into October, straight into the mud and then the winter that broke it at the gates of the city.

That was already the resources first instinct at work, on a small scale.

Baku is a completely different order of problem. Moscow sat about a thousand kilometers from the June 1941 start lines. Baku sat well over twice that, through Ukraine, across the Don, then through the Caucasus range itself, terrain with a handful of usable passes where defenders can bleed an armored spearhead white. 

German supply already rested on horse transport and rail lines they had to physically re-gauge as they advanced, and it was buckling at half that distance. Doubling the distance doesn't strain the system. It ends it.

And we don't have to speculate, because Berlin tried it in 1942 under better conditions than 1941 could ever have offered. Rail lines already converted through occupied Ukraine. A Red Army already bled white by the previous year's disasters. Only one mobile offensive to fuel instead of three, with Army Group Center ordered to sit still and Leningrad held under blockade rather than assaulted, which costs far less in fuel and panzers than an active drive.

With all that concentration, here's what they got. Rostov on 23 July. Maikop's oilfields on 9 August. Then Soviet resistance and the distance from supply bases ground the advance down to local gains. Grozny never fell. 

Baku was never even approached. Maikop had produced around 19 million barrels a year before the war, and after capture the demolition work was so thorough the Germans pulled almost nothing out of it. Furthest any German patrol got toward the Caspian was a rail line near Kizlyar. Nalchik marked the actual limit. Then Sixth Army was encircled at Stalingrad in November and the whole southern gamble came apart.

If the mature 1942 attempt couldn't reach Baku with every advantage, a premature 1941 lunge for it isn't worth crediting with better odds.

There's also a bigger point ! Over fifteen hundred enterprises were pulled beyond the Urals in the second half of 1941 alone and had them producing again within months. That's not a logistics footnote, it's a war winning act, and no arrow drawn on a map in Berlin was going to outrun that kind of strategic depth.

Worth flagging the other side: plenty of historians take the Kiev detour more seriously as a genuine missed chance than I do here. Van Creveld's work on Wehrmacht logistics goes the opposite direction and argues Barbarossa was unsupportable on any axis, Moscow included. He has his own critics who think he sets the ceiling too low. It's a live debate and worth reading into!

Visited Nathu-La, once a key pass of the ancient Silk Route, after a gap of 25 years. 

Remarkably striking infrastructural and connectivity work has taken place since 2015. We also traced the old single lane motorable road from Gangtok to Nathu-La which we had used in 2001. 

Exemplary work is being done by the Indian Army in these forbidding heights. Salute to the commitment, determination and dynamism of its personnel. Resumption of border trade from August 2026, breathes a new life again into this ancient route. 

Standing at this crucial and strategic pass, one cannot but help contemplate on how civilisational Bharat defined and shaped the Silk Route - through which flowed ideas, art, trade and commerce - across the ancient world. 

Iconic scholar Rahul Sankrityayan perhaps best described Bharat’s civilisational flow and outpouring against great odds when he wrote: 

“Roads between India and China and Tibet were extremely dangerous; big deserts had to be crossed where there was no bird  in the air or animal on the ground, and so the track was very difficult to find. About two in ten could reach the destination - the rest would become victims of pestilence and pirates, slippery passes and swift rivers, dacoits and famines…It was the fervour of idealism, the spirit of self-sacrifice and defiance of death that were at the root of the spread of Indian culture in these distant lands. Let us offer our homage to the memory of those selfless saintly scholars and pray that their spirit may once more animate the soul of modern India, so that she may once more rise to a glorious place in the comity of nations.” 

(Rahul Sankrityayan, Selected Essays, 1984) #NathuLa

text:
How Charlie Kirk secretly saved my family...
We lived in a rough neighborhood in D.C. It was the only house we could afford, and we were happy there. We had just brought our firstborn newborn child home when D.C. defunded its police. Our street turned into a war zone overnight, and the neighbor's rowhouse was burned to ashes in a gangland arson that badly damaged our home as well.
My family had nowhere to go. I found my wife standing in the street wrapped in a firefighter's blanket, freezing cold, holding our newborn baby, surrounded by first responders putting out the fire. Everything was a total loss. Charlie Kirk called me within the hour and did something incredible -- he offered us his house to stay in. It was a condo in Sarasota, Florida.
We didn't have the finances to pay for a hotel for months or travel back and forth to D.C. Charlie let us stay for as long as we needed. We spent months in Charlie's Florida condo searching for a new family home of our own -- finally finding the right one, and we moved out of D.C. permanently. Now my family is growing and happy and thriving. This could have never happened without Charlie and Erika's generosity.
Charlie never asked for a thing and never wanted me to tell anyone. Charlie practiced what he preached as a Christian. He never once talked about this with anyone. Pure good Samaritan energy. I know there are many more stories like this...
The only person who truly showed up for us at our lowest moment was Charlie Kirk. A true man of God.
